title: Opinion: Canada’s pension fund whistles past the graveyard as climate risks mount
html:
At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, negotiators removed mention of fossil fuels from their revised deal draft.YASIN AKGUL/AFP/Getty Images

John Rapley is a contributing columnist for The Globe and Mail. He is an author and academic whose books include Why Empires Fall and Twilight of the Money Gods.

At the COP31 summit in Turkey this week, climate action suffered a setback. Negotiators dropped any mention of ending fossil fuel use in their deal text, as cost of living and energy security concerns diverted policy-makers’ attention.

But those who manage money were clearer eyed. Earlier at COP, 40 of the world’s largest pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds warned of the “systemic risk” posed by climate change. As well they might, since a growing body of research is raising concerns about the negative impact extreme weather is already starting to have on asset prices and economic growth, a risk which will only heighten with time.

Then, there’s the Canada Pension Plan, gleefully whistling past that graveyard and sinking its money into fossil fuels while waving off concerns about climate risk. So concerned were a group of young Canadians that their future retirements might be in jeopardy as a result that they enlisted the advocacy group Ecojustice and law firm Goldblatt Partners to launch a suit against the CPP Investment Board.

The case, which was heard last week in the Ontario Superior Court, alleged that the board was subjecting contributors who would retire in the more distant future, when the effects of climate change will be most manifest, to undue risk of loss. It’s a strong case: You would normally expect investment funds with 75-year time horizons to pay a good deal of attention to risks that are likely to materialize in that time frame, particularly if they could negatively affect their investment portfolios, and yet the CPP looks to have taken a rather cavalier approach to the matter.

Canada’s largest pension fund – and one of the biggest in the world – is well known in the industry for downplaying the dangers posed by climate change. As the advocacy group Shift: Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health pointed out recently, “CPPIB has no disclosed climate action plan, no net-zero emissions commitment, no targets to reduce portfolio emissions, weak evidence of effective climate engagement with investee companies, no goals to invest more in profitable climate solutions, and no exclusions on investment in oil, gas and coal.”

One could argue that it’s not the role of the CPP to accelerate the energy transition nor phase out oil and gas, a topic on which Canadians are in any case divided. However, in assessing the fund’s long-term solvency, it is incumbent on any fund manager to take stock of both potential risks to its asset base and the future macroeconomic environment in which its contributors will be working. For decades, fund managers largely neglected climate change. But in light of the rapid increase in both the number of extreme weather events and their economic toll, incorporating climate risk into investment analysis has become common practice.

You’d be hard-pressed to find that sense of urgency in the CPP’s own reports, though. It uses a model that estimates that in a worst-case scenario, in which there is little change from the current global trajectory in carbon emissions and the world becomes much warmer, the hit to the market value of its assets would amount to a mere 4 per cent.

This is, to put it politely, optimistic. It also looks seriously outdated. When modelling the economic impact of climate change first emerged as a serious topic of study about 30 years ago, these were the sorts of estimates researchers came up with for an optimistic scenario, in which global warming was kept below 1.5 C.

Since then, though, the scholarly literature has evolved considerably. In particular, the much greater severity of extreme weather has altered the approaches used by economists, and estimates of much bigger damages are becoming commonplace. Indeed, Canada knows this better than most, as wildfires actually knocked 1.3 per cent off the economy’s growth rate in 2023, roughly cutting it in half.

That’s why other pension funds have scrapped the sort of methodology still being used by the CPP. The world’s largest pension fund, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, said the model in question produced “implausibly low loss estimates even for higher temperature scenarios.” AXA Insurance has similarly said that the model “does not account for the sustainability of the infrastructure, grids or other necessary components that enable the assets to operate and generate revenue.”

Canada’s Office of the Chief Actuary, an independent unit within the federal financial regulator, has taken issue with the CPP’s estimates and says that in a business-as-usual or worst-case scenario, the hit to Canadian GDP could amount to 30 per cent by 2100, an estimate echoed in a widely cited academic paper earlier this year.

Yet while the scholarship has moved on, the CPP Investment Board is clinging to old theories and, rather like a creationist before the vast body of evidence on evolution, opting to ignore the current science. Canadians, especially younger Canadians, may find their retirements rendered less comfortable by this complacency. Whether it thinks it has any duty to answer to Canadians for its choices, the board should be made to do so.
summary: The plan continues to sink its money into fossil fuels while waving off climate risk concerns
